coredata.dc:description: An optimized process using amorphous silica for efficient C3S synthesis in the laboratory is reported: an estimated production capacity of ~2 kg C3S within a week is possible. Amorphous silica (fumed silica) was used as raw material and inter-ground with CaCO3 and water for C3S synthesis, the dried raw mixture has sufficient green strength to be self-supporting, which allows large cylinders to be placed in Platinum crucibles. The mineral composition of the sintered sample was quantified with X-ray powder diffraction using Rietveld analysis. C3S with <0.4 wt% of free CaO was sintered at a shortened residence time (≤5 h) when temperatures ≥1550 °C. The efficiency of the C3S synthesis was dramatically enhanced because of 1) increased burnability of the raw mix due to amorphous silica and very fine CaCO3 particles after grinding, 2) simplified sample preparation process avoiding pressing discs and 3) improved capacities of the crucible and furnace.

ce:abstract-sec.ce:simple-para: An optimized process using amorphous silica for efficient C3S synthesis in the laboratory is reported: an estimated production capacity of ~2 kg C3S within a week is possible. Amorphous silica (fumed silica) was used as raw material and inter-ground with CaCO3 and water for C3S synthesis, the dried raw mixture has sufficient green strength to be self-supporting, which allows large cylinders to be placed in Platinum crucibles. The mineral composition of the sintered sample was quantified with X-ray powder diffraction using Rietveld analysis. C3S with <0.4 wt% of free CaO was sintered at a shortened residence time (≤5 h) when temperatures ≥1550 °C. The efficiency of the C3S synthesis was dramatically enhanced because of 1) increased burnability of the raw mix due to amorphous silica and very fine CaCO3 particles after grinding, 2) simplified sample preparation process avoiding pressing discs and 3) improved capacities of the crucible and furnace.

ce:section.ce:para: C3S (tricalcium silicate) is the major phase in Portland cement, as such many studies have been focused on the reaction of this phase alone. However, more extensive work is hindered by the difficulty in obtaining high quality C3S. It is important to realise that C3S, like Portland cement will tend to age, due to humidity in the atmosphere, if stored for too long. The best quality materials can be obtained if it is synthesized fresh for each study. Furthermore, local synthesis allows adjustment of the minor elements to obtain alite with grain growth similar to alite in Portland cement, which can then be ground to have a particle size distribution resembling Portland cement. However, most of the standard methods for preparing C3S are very time-consuming.

Here we report the straightforward synthesis of kilogram quantities of C3S which adapts the solid reaction method [1,21] and can be used in any laboratory equipped with a high-temperature furnace. The solid reaction routine was modified by changing the raw materials and procedures to maximize the furnace efficiency and decrease the workload of the procedures. The sintering parameters were optimized to maximize the amount of C3S which could be produced within working hours.

A correction of the mix design was needed based on actual mineral composition detected by X-ray powder diffraction (XRD) or the actual chemical composition by X-ray fluorescence (XRF) of the trial mix design. The reason for the deviation in chemical composition was moisture/solvent residue in fumed silicas so there was less SiO2 than expected in the weighed quantity. Extra amount silica will be needed to react with the excess f-CaO to compensate for this effect. The excess 3.7 wt% of CaO (by mass 476.67 g × 0.037 = 17.80 g) was compensated by 6.44 g of silica in the mix to form C3S, resulting 133.11 g of silica.

The required equipment/tools are (see Fig. 2 ):
•
ball milling jar up to 3 L
•
milling balls (ZrO2) with diameter ~30 mm
•
rolling machine to grind by rotating the ball milling jar
•
cylinder moulds 1
1 Depend on the size of the platinum crucible and the inside height of the furnace, in this paper the ASTM moulds with the dimension of φ70mm × 140 mm for mortar test was used
•
ladles, filters and containers (i.e. salad spinner) to separate the ball and mixed raw materials
•
high-temperature furnace (up to at least 1600 °C)
•
Pt crucible
•
strengthened crucible tongs with extra-long handle and a fire proof base
•
fan for cooling process (cleaned compressed air can be used as well)
•
a full set of protection such as heat resistance gloves, welding glasses and heat resistant helmet
The details of the analytical techniques used: X-ray powder diffraction; Rietveld analysis, particle size distribution and scanning electron microscopy (SEM) are given in the annex.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Method (video can be found in Supplementary material)

ce:section.ce:para:
The raw materials were weighed according to the steps stated previously in the materials section (Section 2.1) as shown in Table 4. A summarized schematic plot of the procedures is shown in Fig. 3. Figs. 4 and 5 shows the pictures for the casting of the raw cylinder, the sintering and the quenching of the samples. More detailed steps for sample preparation are:
•
Step 1:
◦
Add grinding balls (2.4 kg of ~5 cm ZrO2 ball) into the cleaned jar (volume up to 3 L);
◦
Weigh exact amount of SiO2 into the jar; then add CaCO3 and other oxides (i.e. Al2O3, MgO and Fe2O3 for alite synthesis) when necessary (see Table 4);
◦
Add ~1.5 kg (mass ratio of water/materials ~2.0) of distilled water
•
Step 2 2
2 Here we provide an example way of grinding. Any other grinding method (i.e. planetary ball mill) which can reduce the PSD of the raw materials can be used. :
◦
Close the jar before putting it on a rolling machine for 24 h for a homogeneous mixing; remove any material stuck on the lid into the jar by interrupting the milling 2–3 times;
•
Step 3:
◦
Filter the paste using salad spinner by manually shaking interior colander
◦
Transfer the paste into cylinder moulds (φ70mm × 140 mm);
•
Step 4:
◦
Dry the blends at 105 °C until constant weight (~48 h, maybe longer), make sure the cylinders are completely dried, as the moisture residue in the raw cylinders would cause damage to the furnace;
•
Step 5:
◦
Place the dried cylinder into the clean Pt crucible carefully;
•
Step 6:
◦
Carefully transport the sample together with the Pt crucible into the furnace, make sure there is enough space between the crucibles to take them out of the furnace (see Fig. 4);
◦
After required sintering time, handle the sample with full set of high-temperature protection, quench the sintered C3S using forced air (see Fig. 5).

The sintering temperature of 1450, 1500, 1550 and 1600 °C was used coupled with residence times of 2.5, 5, 10, 15 and 20 h, respectively. A summary of the parameters is shown in Table 5. After sintering, C3S was cooled down in the forced air with a fan.

Make sure the cylinders are completely dry before putting them into the furnace, otherwise any moisture in the samples risks damaging the heating units and refractory materials inside the furnace. Make sure the green cylinder was standing still in the Pt crucible without any following pieces out of the crucible, open the furnace to check the status of the reacting cylinders once or twice, especially for the first few sintering experiments. Wear welding glasses, heat resistance helmet/head mask, chest protection, lab coat, safety shoes and heat resistance gloves when handling samples at high temperature. Special care must be taken to avoid touching the heating units when taking the sample in and out, which are extremely fragile.

The potential danger of fumed silica is inhalation hazardous, skin and/or eye contact according to OSHA (Occupational Safety and Health Administration) [22]. In inhalation studies, none of the examined synthetic amorphous silica led to durable changes in the lung or to progressive damage comparable to silicosis [23,24]. However, when exposed to high concentration (3 mg/m3), there could be a danger to life or health according to NIOSH (The National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health) [25]. The important steps for the protection are: wear N95 mask (FFP3 mask when nano powders are involved), safety glasses, hygienic cap, lab coat, gloves, and handle the fumed silica in the ventilation hood. The waste powder should be cleaned with a piece of wet cloth or paper.

Fumed silica (amorphous) with larger particle size (>100 nm, i.e. 0.2 μm) was recommended to avoid handling nano particles. Constituent particles in the size range 1–100 nm was considered nano particles [26]. As long as SiO2 powder was mixed with water, there is no more danger. Principally, the rules for handling nano-particles must be followed according to the specific protocols from the institution/laboratory if nano fumed silica is used, for more details the reader is referred to the paper by Groso et al. [27].
The characteristic ranges of the XRD pattern accompanied by the Rietveld fitting (as shown in Fig. 6 ) showed the presence of T1 polymorph for C3S [28–30].

The quantitative Rietveld results from the different sintering temperatures and residence times (shown in Table 5) were compiled into contour plots of the C3S and f-CaO (free lime) content as shown in Fig. 7 . These can be used to determine conditions for practical sintering [31–33]. For instance, a sample with ~96 wt% C3S and ~0.3 wt% f-CaO can be sintered at point P1, P2 or P3 as shown in Fig. 7. So, the sintering can be done with a short resistance time (≤5 h) for temperatures ≥1550 °C or a longer time (≥10 h) for temperatures ≤1500 °C. The practical choice of the sintering temperature depends on the length of the working day and the model of the furnace available. Near identical results were obtained for both the silicas used (see Table 5).

Samples from different places of the cylinder were taken to check the homogeneity of the sintered C3S (as shown in Table 5). There was no significant difference in the mineral composition for samples taken from different positions. Micrographs of the raw mix and the sintered C3S (Fig. 8 (a) and (b)) also show good homogeneity.

For most of the study, a heating speed of 5° per minute was used, but a faster heating speed of 7 °C/min had no negative impact on the quality of the C3S (see Table 5). This faster heating speed decreases the total synthesis time to 6.7 h which can be fitted into a normal working day when C3S is sintered at 1600 °C for 3 h (point P3 in Fig. 7). This avoids using the furnace overnight. For most of high-temperature furnaces (up to 1600–1700 °C), a heating speed of 7 °C /min is practical, as 5–10 °C/min is usually recommended.

Here, a simplified process for C3S synthesis is reported, using amorphous silica and avoiding pressing raw mix into discs. This greatly increases the efficiency of C3S synthesis at the laboratory scale. The sintering can be done at short resistance times (≤5 h) when temperatures ≥1550 °C are used.
A detailed comparison of the protocols used for C3S synthesis is summarized in Table 6 .

The capacity of the C3S synthesis under these conditions was ~2 kg/week which was 5–10 times more than that from the traditional routine (see Table 6). The quality of the final C3S was good (with 96–98 wt% of C3S and f-CaO <0.4 wt%).

The dried cast cylinder is porous which promotes the escape of CO2 inside of the cylinder during the decomposition of the CaCO3. The resulting C3S blocks were also porous (see Fig. 8 (b)) and easy to grind.

The main aspects of improvement are (see Table 2 and Fig. 3):
•
Raw mix preparation: use cast cylinders instead of pressed discs.
•
Sintering time: improved burnability as the use of amorphous silica and decreased PSD for calcium carbonate by grinding
•
Capacity of the crucible and furnace: increased capacity as the use of cast cylinders.
The Dv50 of the calcite was decreased from 16 μm to ~4 μm after grinding (see Table 3). The simplified process by casting the paste into cylinder contributed to the capacity of the C3S synthesis.

Alite doped with oxides (i.e. Fe2O3, Al2O3, ZnO, MgO etc.) could also be produced using the procedure reported here. The homogeneity of the alite doped with chemicals with high dissolution rates in water (i.e. alkali, gypsum etc.) must be checked before moving to the massive synthesis. This is also the case when using colloidal silica (i.e. Ludox® GRACE, Sigma-Aldrich) as the source of SiO2, as colloidal silica typically contains relative high sodium content. Because the water migration and evaporation during the drying process of the raw mix might cause some inhomogeneity of these samples. The process reported here for alite synthesis could be used for belite at a lowered sintering temperature, typically at 1350 °C.

ce:section.ce:label: A.2
ce:section.ce:section-title: X-ray powder diffraction and Rietveld analysis
ce:section.ce:para: Approximately 5 g of powder was ground by hand for XRD analysis using mortar and pestle. X-ray powder diffraction (XRD) data were collected using PANalytical X'pert pro working at 45 kV and 40 mA immediately after the C3S was sintered to avoid hydration. Incident beam Soller slits of 0.04 rad were used and the incident divergence and antiscatter slits were fixed at 0.5°. Air scattering was reduced using a beam knife. The receiving antiscatter slit was fixed at 1° and receiving Soller slits limiting the axial divergence to 0.04 rad were positioned in the diffracted beam path. An X'Celerator linear position-sensitive X-ray detector was used for data acquisition. Powder samples were backloaded and measured with an accumulated time per step of 60 s, resulting in a total measurement time of about 30 min per scan. Samples were scanned on a spinning sample stage between 5 and 65° with 0.017°2θ step size.

Rietveld analysis was made using TOPAS academic (version 6.0). The refined parameters are background, sample displacement, scale, unit cell and Lorentz crystal size (fundamental profile describing the peak shape [34]). The crystal structures used were: T1 polymorph for C3S (ICSD No. 4331) [28], beta C2S (ICSD No. 81096) [35] and f-CaO (ICSD No. 75786). Average weighed residue Rwp was ~10% for the refinements.

ce:section.ce:label: A.3
ce:section.ce:para: Particle size distribution (PSD) was measured using a Malvern Master Sizer device. Powdered samples were dispersed using ultrasonic horn and magnetic stirrer in isopropanol for 15 min. The reflection index of the CaCO3 and the raw mix were set to 1.6.

ce:section.ce:label: A.4
ce:section.ce:para: Blocks of samples and pressed discs made with powders were impregnated into the resin under vacuum. The polished section was coated with ~14 nm carbon before the SEM. Backscattered electron images were taken using 15 kV accelerating voltage with a working distance of 10 mm at a spot size of 4.2 on a FEI QUANTA 200 microscopy.
